teaching.task: # Year 12 Physics M5 V15: Work in circular motion. Does the inward force do work in uniform circular motion? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Remember what work is. A force does work when it pushes something along the direction it moves. The work is the force, times the displacement, times the cosine of the angle between them. Push along the motion, and the angle is zero, so all of the force counts. Push at right angles to the motion, and the angle is ninety degrees. Cosine ninety is zero, so that force does no work at all. Now chop the lap into tiny steps. In each step, the car moves a tiny distance along the tangent. But the inward force points at the centre, at right angles to that step. So in every step, the work done is zero. Add up zero, step after step, and the total over a whole lap is zero too. The one point two six million joules assumed the force pointed along the path. It never does. That fits with the work-energy theorem. The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy. Zero work means the kinetic energy doesn't change, so the speed doesn't change. The car's kinetic energy is a half m v squared, about a hundred thousand joules, and it stays at that value lap after lap. If one point two six million joules really went in each lap, the car would be going more than three times faster after just one lap.

scenes.teachingReason: From the top to the bottom, the stone drops two radii, one point zero metre. So v squared at the bottom is nine, plus two times nine point eight times one point zero, which is twenty-eight point six, and v is about five point three five metres per second. Gravity has a part along the path, so it does work and the speed changes. That's why the motion isn't uniform. The slip is saying the speed stays at three point zero, because the tension does no work. Gravity still does.

scenes.teachingReason: So F equals m v squared over r tells us the inward force a circle needs, and that force does no work. But how do we know the formula is right? We can test it. Here's a rubber bung on a string. The string runs down through a short glass tube, to some hanging masses. The hanging weight keeps the string tight, and pulls the bung inwards. So can measurements of this bung test F equals m v squared over r?
